disease_info: Adjustment Disorder is characterized by the development of emotional or behavioral symptoms in response to an identifiable psychosocial stressor, with onset typically within three months of the stressor and resulting in distress or impairment that is out of proportion to what would be expected. The disturbance causes clinically significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning but does not meet criteria for another specific mental disorder and is not merely an exacerbation of a preexisting condition. Symptoms are time-limited and usually resolve within six months after the stressor or its consequences have ended, although they can persist if the stressor is ongoing. Clinically, it is differentiated from normal stress reactions by the degree of functional impairment and from disorders like major depression or anxiety disorders by its tighter temporal relationship to a stressor and generally milder, more situational course.

narrative.stressor: About six weeks before presenting, Garrett’s construction company lost a major contract, and management abruptly shifted several crew members, cutting his hours and assigning him more paperwork-heavy tasks he had never been trained for. He was passed over for a crew lead role he had been informally promised, with supervisors citing his missed paperwork and "lack of organization" despite his strong on-site skills. The combination of reduced income, fear of being laid off, and daily criticism about forms and deadlines left him feeling increasingly out of step with the fast-changing expectations at work, to the point that he started skipping rec league games and turning down weekend projects with friends because he felt he "couldn’t keep up with anything." After a month of deteriorating performance and a written warning from his foreman, his sister urged him to see a mental health professional when he admitted that the stress from the workplace changes was starting to spill over into every part of his life.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Ever since they cut my hours and dumped all this paperwork on me, I just haven’t been handling it well and I feel like I’m reacting all wrong to everything at work.”

narrative.stressor: Roughly a month before seeking help, Gilda’s primary source of income—a series of pop-up art events sponsored by a local gallery—was abruptly canceled when the gallery closed under new ownership, leaving her without the modest but steady payments she relied on to cover rent and studio supplies. Because she tends to manage money informally and sometimes forgets bills, the sudden loss of income led to late notices, mounting fees, and a tense meeting with her landlord about possible eviction if she fell further behind. As she scrambled to design new freelance offerings and apply for part-time work outside her creative field, she found that the financial pressure was starting to overshadow her usual sense of calm curiosity, and she began avoiding her sketching circles and gallery visits because they reminded her of the stalled career plans. When a close friend pointed out how unlike herself she seemed and offered to go with her, Gilda agreed to consult a clinician, worried that her reactions to the financial setback were starting to interfere with her ability to function day to day.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Losing that gallery income has thrown me off so much that I feel like I’m not handling the money stress in a normal way anymore.”

narrative.stressor: About a month before his evaluation, Jeffrey’s wife told him she was seriously considering a separation after months of feeling sidelined by his long hours and constant preoccupation with clients, and she suggested a trial period living apart while they "figured things out." The announcement came just as he was finalizing a high-stakes contract for a marquee client, forcing him to juggle complex negotiations with the sudden destabilization of his home life and new logistical issues around shared parenting time. Despite his usual preference for structure and planning, he found himself fixating on the potential dissolution of the marriage, second-guessing every interaction at home, and increasingly unable to maintain his usual level of focus and predictability in meetings and on the golf course. After his performance metrics slipped, a colleague privately commented that he seemed "off his game" and his wife reiterated that he needed to address how he was reacting to the separation talks, prompting Jeffrey to seek psychiatric consultation when he realized his response to the marital crisis was beginning to undermine both his family relationships and his work.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Ever since my wife brought up separating, I feel like I’m not coping with it well at all and it’s throwing off how I function at home and at work.”
